newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Sinn Fein denies report of unofficial IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein denies report of unofficial IRA truce.

text.p: A key figure in Sinn Fein, political wing of the IRA guerrilla movement, on Sunday denied a press report that the guerrillas were observing an unofficial truce to secure better terms at Northern Ireland peace talks.

Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's top negotiator, told Irish radio there was "no truth whatsoever" to the report in Dublin's Sunday Tribune newspaper, the latest in a series suggesting that a new ceasefire was imminent, possibly in time for Christmas.

The newspaper said Irish Republican Army guerrillas had observed the truce since they bombed Britain's Northern Ireland army base at Lisburn, outside Belfast, killing one soldier and injuring 30 on October 7.

The aim of the truce was to enhance mediation efforts between Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams and the British and Irish governments by John Hume, leader of Northern Ireland's Social, Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), the paper said.
But McGuinness said that, as far as he knew, a 17-month IRA truce ended in February and the guerrillas were still at war to end British rule of Northern Ireland and unite it with Ireland.

"I am working on the basis that the IRA cessation ended on February 9, and since then John Hume and Gerry Adams have been working with others to attempt to restore a meaningful peace process and put in place a credible process of negotiations," McGuinness said.
He repeated Sinn Fein's view that Britain had "squandered" the IRA's 17-month truce by placing preconditions on Sinn Fein's entry into the peace talks.

The British and Irish governments have banned all ministerial contact with Sinn Fein since the ending of the IRA ceasefire in February and say only a new truce will allow Sinn Fein to join other parties at peace talks under way in Belfast.

Senior figures in the Irish republican movement, which seeks to end British rule of Northern Ireland and reunite the province with Ireland, were predicting renewed violence unless the talks' terms were eased, the Sunday Tribune said.
Britain's Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, and Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, meet in Belfast on Wednesday to discuss the talks, which started, without Sinn Fein, last June.

The Tribune said the IRA observed several similar unofficial ceasefires in the run-up to an August 1994 "total cessation" of its guerrilla war which helped open the door to the most intense effort to end the Northern Ireland conflict in 27 years.
Last week Mayhew and McGuinness gave speeches which were seen as coded dialogue about what each side expected from the other to secure a new IRA truce and a Sinn Fein talks' seat.
Mayhew said an IRA truce would have to be matched by deeds if Britain was to have any faith in a new ceasefire. The London government wants assurances that a new truce will be permanent.

McGuinness said that Sinn Fein would not try to seek a new IRA truce unless Britain set a credible time-frame for the talks and dropped what he said were preconditions aimed at getting the IRA to surrender its guerrilla arsenal.
Sin Fein's arch-foes, Protestant Unionist parties which want the province to stay British, insist that the IRA must agree to surrender arms to prove a commitment to democratic means.

Under the terms of the talks, participants must pledge loyalty to a set of principles on non-violence and democracy and Unionists, which represent the province's 60 percent Protestant majority, insist that this means a surrender of weapons.
